Expert implementation code is withheld. 2.3 Expert Design Guidance Expert design guidance connects algorithmic choices to their implementation. In the guided configuration, this guidance is made available to the agent alongside the shared task files defined in Section 2.2 . Expert code supplies the design choices; corresponding technical documentation and comments clarify their intent. We organize the guidance into three levels: • L1 : High-level algorithmic insights. Such guidance states the algorithmic transformation, why the proposed algorithmic insight would preserve the operator’s required behavior, and the computation or data movement it could optimize. • L2 : Dataflow design. The guidance specifies where variables should be produced, stored, and consumed, together with their layouts and lifetimes. The guidance also identifies intermediate variables that can be reused or avoided. • L3 : Low-level optimization tricks. The guidance explains how execution mechanisms implement the design, such as optimizing pipelining to overlap data movement with computation and warp specialization to assign different roles to warps. The guidance also specifies the required ordering and synchronization while leaving concrete tuning parameters unspecified. The guidance records dependencies among the three levels to explain how the design choices work together. These dependencies connect an algorithmic transformation to the data representation and movement it requires, and then to the GPU execution mechanisms that preserve its benefits. They specify the cross-level dependencies among algorithmic, dataflow, and low-level execution choices, including the required ordering and state transitions. Example expert guidance for Muon orthogonalization kernel. We provide the corresponding example of the expert guidance for the Muon orthogonalization kernel. The Muon guidance replaces repeated updates of the large rectangular matrix with composition on smaller square matrices (Figure 1 (b) ). At L1 , the guidance defines 𝐏 k = a k ​ 𝐈 + b k ​ 𝐑 k + c k ​ 𝐑 k 2 \mathbf{P}_{k}=a_{k}\mathbf{I}+b_{k}\mathbf{R}_{k}+c_{k}\mathbf{R}_{k}^{2} . In exact arithmetic, since 𝐗 k + 1 = 𝐏 k ​ 𝐗 k \mathbf{X}_{k+1}=\mathbf{P}_{k}\mathbf{X}_{k} , steps 0 0 through j j can be composed into 𝐐 = 𝐏 j ⋯ 𝐏 0 \mathbf{Q}=\mathbf{P}_{j}\cdots\mathbf{P}_{0} . The resulting rectangular matrix is then computed as 𝐗 j + 1 = 𝐐𝐗 0 \mathbf{X}_{j+1}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{X}_{0} in a single matrix multiplication, avoiding explicit computation of the intermediate rectangular matrices 𝐗 1 , … , 𝐗 j \mathbf{X}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{X}_{j} . Meanwhile, the Gram matrix is updated directly as 𝐑 k + 1 = 𝐏 k ​ 𝐑 k ​ 𝐏 k ⊤ \mathbf{R}_{k+1}=\mathbf{P}_{k}\mathbf{R}_{k}\mathbf{P}_{k}^{\top} , rather than recomputed as 𝐗 k + 1 ​ 𝐗 k + 1 ⊤ \mathbf{X}_{k+1}\mathbf{X}_{k+1}^{\top} . This algorithmic transformation preserves the result in exact arithmetic while replacing repeated rectangular-matrix updates with composition on smaller square matrices. At L2 , the dataflow keeps rectangular 𝐗 \mathbf{X} fixed throughout each composition segment, while square states 𝐑 \mathbf{R} and 𝐐 \mathbf{Q} are updated and reused across consecutive polynomial steps. The updated rectangular matrix is materialized only at the segment boundary by applying 𝐐 \mathbf{Q} to 𝐗 \mathbf{X} . Before step k = 2 k{=}2 , the fixed restart applies the composition of steps 0 and 1 to 𝐗 \mathbf{X} , rounds to FP16 , rebuilds 𝐑 = 𝐗𝐗 ⊤ \mathbf{R}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^{\top} to limit numerical drift, and initializes a fresh 𝐐 = a 2 ​ 𝐈 + b 2 ​ 𝐑 + c 2 ​ 𝐑 2 \mathbf{Q}=a_{2}\mathbf{I}+b_{2}\mathbf{R}+c_{2}\mathbf{R}^{2} for steps 2 through 4. At L3 , the kernel execution schedule respects these data dependencies: square-state matrix-product kernels execute within each segment, and rectangular products apply 𝐐 \mathbf{Q} at restart and final boundaries after the corresponding square-state updates are complete. To avoid redundant arithmetic, symmetric-product kernels compute one triangle and reuse each tile’s accumulator for the original and transposed stores, writing diagonal tiles only once. For each task, we prepare two LLM-judge prompts: one assesses an independently generated written design, and the other assesses generated implementation code. The written design is elicited in a separate agent run described in Section 3.3 . Both judge prompts combine the task description, task-specific design criteria, and shared assessment instructions. These criteria form the design specification, describing the expert’s design choices, the costs they remove, and the requirements for combining them correctly. The design-assessment prompt includes the agent’s written design; the implementation-assessment prompt includes the three levels of guidance, the expert implementation, and the candidate source code. The scoring procedure is described in Section 3.3 . 3 Evaluation Protocol We describe the agentic evaluation pipeline with and without expert design guidance (Section 3.1 ), define the measured performance score S perf \mathrm{S}_{\text{perf}} (Section 3.2 ), and define the LLM judge scores for independent designs, JS design \mathrm{JS}_{\text{design}} , and generated implementations, JS impl \mathrm{JS}_{\text{impl}} (Section 3.3 ). 3.1 Agentic Evaluation Pipeline For each model and task, we conduct paired agentic optimization runs with and without expert design guidance. Each run follows the same pipeline: task initialization, iterative kernel optimization and evaluation, and final submission selection. Figure 2 illustrates the agent loop and its interaction with the evaluator sandbox. Task initialization. Each agentic execution starts with an agent workspace containing the shared task files defined in Section 2.2 . The guided run additionally receives the expert design guidance from Section 2.3 , covering all three levels, together with instructions. This additional input is represented by the dashed branch in Figure 2 . Expert source code is unavailable to the agent in both runs. The two runs otherwise use the same implementation language, tools, hardware, and optimization budget. Iterative kernel optimization and evaluation. The agent develops candidate implementations by editing the supplied solution.py template shown in Figure 1 (a) . The template specifies the task-specific signature of run(...) and leaves the function body unimplemented; the agent implements this function to produce the required outputs and state updates. The agent interacts with the execution sandbox through Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools: read and write support file inspection and implementation editing, bash executes compilation and profiling commands, and submit invokes the evaluator. On submission, the evaluator loads the candidate file and calls run(...) with inputs prepared for each workload according to the task description. The agent uses the returned correctness and timing feedback, together with profiling tools such as NVIDIA Nsight Compute ( ncu ), to diagnose bottlenecks and revise its implementation. This process forms an iterative loop of implementation, compilation, testing, profiling, and revision. Final submission selection. Both runs use the same fixed turn limit and selection procedure. One agent turn consists of a model response requesting one or more tool calls, execution of those calls, and return of their results. A candidate is eligible for final selection only if the candidate passes the correctness and implementation checks and has valid latency measurements on every workload of the task. For each eligible candidate, we compute the geometric mean of its speedups across the task’s workloads, as defined in Section 3.2 . Among eligible candidates produced within the turn limit, we select the one with the highest geometric mean speedup as the final submission. Figure 2 : Evaluation workflow. The dashed branch supplies L1 – L3 guidance in the guided run. MCP calls and feedback use separate arrows. The LLM judge assigns an implementation score at each level; the arithmetic mean of these scores is JS impl \mathrm{JS}_{\text{impl}} . The evaluator measures S perf \mathrm{S}_{\text{perf}} . 3.2 Objective Evaluation Metrics We include an objective evaluation module (shown in Figure 2 ) to check correctness and implementation validity, measure latency, and compute performance scores for submitted implementations. Correctness and implementation validity. A task is scored as correct only if its submission satisfies both the correctness criteria and implementation requirements on every workload. Violations of the implementation requirements count as incorrect even when numerical outputs are correct. Correctness checks cover numerical outputs, updates to mutable inputs, repeated execution on new inputs, and, where applicable, distributed behavior. We check compliance with the custom-kernel requirements in Section 2.2 using abstract syntax tree (AST) analysis, static keyword scans, and inspection of libraries linked during compilation. For distributed tasks, we inspect communication traffic to verify that the required communication occurs. Manual review and unit tests check compliance with the full task description, including all required outputs and state updates. Execution latency timing. We measure GPU execution time for one call to the candidate run(...) entry point, including its kernels and required communication. Input construction, compilation, and evaluator setup are excluded from the timed region. The evaluator controls input preparation and state restoration to provide equivalent inputs to all implementations. For distributed tasks, the reported latency is the maximum across participating ranks. All implementations of a given workload use the same timing procedure. For tasks with very short kernel execution times, such as decoding, we capture repeated calls to run(...) in a CUDA Graph that takes at least one second to execute and replay the graph five times. For other tasks, we use CUDA events to time batches of repeated calls to run(...) , with each batch lasting at least one second. In both modes, the reported latency is the arithmetic mean of repeated per-call measurements. Performance scoring. We evaluate correctness on all 26 tasks for each model and input configuration. We therefore use Qwen3.8-Max-0902 as an LLM judge (Figure 2 ) to assess generated code and independent design proposals against the expert-derived design specification in Section 2.3 . Implementation assessment. For each task and input configuration, the judge assesses the generated code at L1 (algorithmic insights), L2 (dataflow design), and L3 (low-level optimization), as defined in Section 2.3 . Each level is scored from 0 to 100 using five anchors: absent (0), isolated fragments (25), partial implementation (50), substantial implementation (75), and complete implementation (100). Intermediate scores are permitted, and every score must be supported by exact code passages demonstrating the implemented design choices. Runtime measurements are hidden from the judge. Alternative implementations receive credit when they satisfy the assessed design intent, even if they differ from the expert code. Functional correctness is evaluated separately in Section 3.2 . The implementation judge score JS impl m , c , i ∈ [ 0,100 ] \mathrm{JS}_{\text{impl}}^{m,c,i}\in[0,100] is the arithmetic mean of the three level scores for model m m , configuration c c , and task i i . To include all 26 tasks in implementation comparisons, we assign JS impl m , c , i = 0 \mathrm{JS}_{\text{impl}}^{m,c,i}=0 to an incorrect final submission and set its three level scores to zero. This adjustment uses the separate correctness evaluation, not a runtime-based judgment. Independent design assessment. To assess design formulation, we elicit a written proposal in a separate run without expert guidance or code generation, using the same model configuration and maximum turn budget as kernel generation. The judge evaluates the proposal against task-specific design criteria at L1 , L2 , and L3 . The design judge score JS design m , i ∈ [ 0,100 ] \mathrm{JS}_{\text{design}}^{m,i}\in[0,100] is the arithmetic mean of the three level scores. It has no configuration index because the proposal is elicited only without guidance. Reported metrics. Model judge scores are arithmetic means over all 26 tasks: JS design m = 1 | 𝒯 | ​ ∑ i ∈ 𝒯 JS design m , i , JS impl m , c = 1 | 𝒯 | ​ ∑ i ∈ 𝒯 JS impl m , c , i . \mathrm{JS}_{\text{design}}^{m}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\mathrm{JS}_{\text{design}}^{m,i},\qquad\mathrm{JS}_{\text{impl}}^{m,c}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\mathrm{JS}_{\text{impl}}^{m,c,i}. (4) We aggregate each level in the same way and report implementation scores separately for guided and unguided runs. Overall judge scores are arithmetic means across the five models, whereas overall S perf \mathrm{S}_{\text{perf}} is a geometric mean. We omit indices when context suffices. Section 4.2 tests whether these runtime-blind assessments align with measured kernel performance. The scores describe design quality and implementation completeness; they do not directly estimate speedup. 4 Experiments Our experiments assess the benefits and limits of expert design guidance across five models and 26 kernel tasks. We use a budget of 350 agent turns per task (see Appendix A.2 for the experimental setup). We aim to answer three key research questions: RQ1. How does the comprehensive expert design guidance at all three levels affect correctness and end-to-end kernel performance? (Section 4.1 ); RQ2. How closely do LLM judge scores align with measured end-to-end kernel performance? (Section 4.2 ); and RQ3. How does guidance at L1 , L2 , and L3 affect kernel performance?
